strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practical problem: LLMs' limited ability to generate and debug HLS-compatible C code, and to navigate the HLS directive design space. The proposed workflow (fine-tuned generation, tuning, and debugging agents plus RAG-based error repository) is well motivated.

The verification-oriented data augmentation (VODA) idea — using controlled bug injection verified by the HLS tool to synthesize training pairs with error messages and CoT-style debugging instructions — is a sensible and reusable data-engineering contribution for a low-resource domain.

The evaluation is unusually concrete for an LLM-application paper: 612 test cases across 33 designs and 34 error types for repair, real synthesis on Vitis HLS 2022.1 targeting a specific FPGA (ZCU106), comparison against general LLMs, a retrieval-augmented method (RALAD), DSL-based (Dahlia, HeteroCL, Allo) and learning-based (HGBO-DSE) baselines, plus an ablation study decomposing Fixing / +Analysis / +DPO / full pipeline.

Reported results are internally consistent in the sense that the ablation traces the source of gains (fine-tuning, DPO, and iterative multi-agent evaluation), and the claim that test designs were held out of the training distribution is explicitly stated.
Training details (base model Llama3-8B, LoRA, optimizer, learning rates, epochs, hardware) are provided at a level that partially supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Fit to ACL is marginal. This is a hardware design automation (EDA) system paper — HLS synthesis, pragmas, FPGA QoR — with the LLM serving as a component. The NLP contribution (multi-agent orchestration, SFT+DPO on synthetic debugging traces) applies well-established techniques without methods that would advance computational linguistics; the paper reads as a DAC/ICCAD submission.

Reproducibility is weak. No code, dataset, prompts, or BugRAG contents are stated as released. The BugRAG taxonomy (34 error types) is only exemplified via 6 entries in Table 1; dataset curation and the 'golden results' testbench construction are described only at a high level. Given that the main empirical claims hinge on the synthesized datasets, this prevents independent verification.

Baseline fairness is questionable for the central claim: HLSFixer (fine-tuned on in-domain synthetic bugs) is compared to unfine-tuned general LLMs (GPT-4o, Llama3.1-8B, DeepSeek-Coder) on error types that the fine-tuned model was specifically trained to repair. The 63% margin over Llama3-8B largely reflects task specialization rather than a novel method; no fine-tuned baseline (e.g., Llama3-8B SFT'd on the same data without the proposed pipeline) is reported. Similarly, HLSTuner is trained on PolyBench-style kernels and then evaluated on PolyBench kernels, so the claimed generalization is thinly supported despite the 'excluded from training distribution' caveat.

Several headline numbers are confusing or under-specified: the abstract's '3.6x average speedup vs SOTA' does not reconcile cleanly with the 16.7x/5.4x figures in Sections on HLSTuner comparisons; Figure 10/11 comparisons against DSL tools (Dahlia, HeteroCL, Allo) conflate language expressivity differences with directive tuning quality. The Energy Efficiency metric in Eq. 2 is an ad-hoc proxy with unjustified functional forms (activation function on latency, exponential penalties) and unspecified gamma.

Key methodology details are missing: how many bug-injection attempts/verifications per sample, how pass/fail of repaired code is checked (C-sim only? co-sim? equivalence checking?), what 'golden results' means for functional verification, how the scoring agent (LLM 6) prompts are constructed, and statistical variance over multiple runs. Error bars are absent from all figures.

Writing quality issues: typos ('Abaltion Study', 'optimzation'), some overclaiming in the abstract relative to the evidence, and dense system figures (Figure 3) that are hard to follow. The related-work positioning against very recent HLS-agent work (e.g., HLSAgent, Gai et al. 2025) is brief.

The 'verification-oriented data augmentation' overlaps conceptually with existing synthetic-bug-generation and data-augmentation work in chip design (Chang et al. 2024 is cited but the delta is not crisply articulated), so the novelty of the central training paradigm is moderate.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: HLS-C generation, error correction, and design-space optimization are genuinely difficult, and the automation targets a documented bottleneck in hardware development.

The verification-oriented data augmentation (VODA) paradigm—closing the loop from verification failures back into fine-tuning data via controlled bug injection—is a sensible and reasonably novel data-construction strategy for a low-resource domain.

The evaluation covers multiple axes: a 612-case repair benchmark spanning three design provenances, per-error-type pass rates, ablations of the analysis agent and DPO, and optimization comparisons against general LLMs, RAG-based (RALAD), DSL-based, and learning-based baselines.
Training details for the fine-tuned models (base model, LoRA, optimizer, learning rates, hardware) are reported, which is better than many system papers of this type.
weaknesses: Scope fit for ACL is weak. The core contribution is hardware design automation (HLS, FPGA QoR, pragmas); the language-model component is a means, not an object of study. There is no linguistic or NLP insight of general interest, and the venue-relevant audience is likely to be found at DAC/ICCAD/MLCAD/ASPLOS-style venues.

Reproducibility is not established. No code, BugRAG entries, prompts, or datasets are stated to be released. The multi-agent architecture involves roughly ten LLM roles, but the paper never specifies which underlying models power the non-fine-tuned agents (LLM 1, 5, 6, 7, 10) or their prompts, making the pipeline impossible to reconstruct.

The headline metrics are hard to reconcile and possibly overstated: the abstract claims a '3.6× average speedup compared to SOTA,' while the results report 5.4× on unseen kernels, 16.7× vs. Dahlia, 1.4× vs. HGBO-DSE, etc. The basis for the aggregate 'SOTA' claim is unclear, and no statistical testing or variance across runs is provided anywhere.

The 'Energy Efficiency' proxy (Eq. 2) is an arbitrary composite: the exponential latency shaping and the γ sensitivity coefficient are unmotivated and γ is never given a value. Reporting this non-standard metric as a primary comparison weakens the optimization claims; standard latency/resource tables would be more credible.

Potential train/test leakage and bias: the error taxonomy (34 types) is built from the same sources used to construct both BugRAG and the test cases, and the manually crafted designs are produced by the authors. There is no third-party test set or blind-case protocol, so the 82.7% figure may not generalize. The evaluation set contains only five PolyBench kernels for the tuner, limiting the strength of the speedup conclusions.

Baseline fairness: a fine-tuned Llama3-8B with task-specific data is compared against untuned general-purpose LLMs on an error taxonomy the authors themselves curated; the comparison therefore conflates domain adaptation with taxonomy familiarity. The related work identifies prior fine-tuning work (Gai et al. 2025) but no head-to-head comparison is given.

Ablations are incomplete: the contribution of BugRAG retrieval and of the multi-agent scoring loop are not isolated, and the DPO gain (+1.8%) is small and reported without confidence intervals. Iterative repair ('up to five iterations') confounds single-attempt capability with retry budget, which is not applied uniformly to baselines.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: redundant Figure 1 rendering, a typos in headings ('Abaltion Study', 'optimzation'), unclear role separation among the many agents in Figure 3, and inconsistent reporting of pass rates (80.8%/86.5% per phase vs. 82.7% overall) require careful decoding.

strengths: The system contribution is substantial and end-to-end: ChatHLS integrates fine-tuned LLMs (SFT + DPO on Llama-3-8B) with HLS tools across generation, debugging (HLSFixer), and optimization (HLSTuner), which is a more complete pipeline than prior RAG-based HLS assistants (e.g., RALAD, HLSPilot).

The VODA verification-oriented data augmentation paradigm is a sensible and potentially reusable idea: systematically injecting verified HLS-specific bugs (via BugRAG error slices) to build fine-tuning data addresses a real data-scarcity problem in the hardware domain.

Evaluation effort is non-trivial: 612 debugging cases spanning 34 error types across Kernel/Vitis/Manual sources, per-error-type pass-rate breakdowns (Figure 6), an ablation isolating the contributions of fine-tuning, DPO, and iterative multi-agent refinement (+8.7%, +1.8%, +8.5%), and comparisons against general LLMs, RAG-based, DSL-based, and learning-based DSE baselines.

The paper is clearly motivated and situates itself well against prior HLS automation (DSLs, heuristic/predictive DSE, RAG-based assistants), and the reported headline numbers (82.7% repair rate; 16.7×/3.5×/2.0×/1.4× over Dahlia/HeteroCL/Allo/HGBO-DSE) are concrete and internally consistent across abstract, results, and conclusion.
weaknesses: Venue fit is a decisive concern for ACL: the core contribution is hardware design automation (HLS/EDA), not computational linguistics or NLP methodology. The LLM techniques used (LoRA SFT, DPO, CoT templating, multi-agent orchestration) are standard and are applied as engineering components toward an EDA goal; the paper reads as a DAC/ICCAD/MLCAD submission. The linguistic/NLP insight is thin, and ACL reviewers will struggle to assess claims like synthesis timing and utilization against their expertise.

Reproducibility is not adequately supported: there is no artifact/code/dataset release statement, the pipeline depends on the proprietary Vitis HLS 2022.1 toolchain and a specific Xilinx ZCU106 board, the fine-tuned checkpoints and BugRAG repository are not described in a way that permits reconstruction, and the multi-agent prompt formats are only partially illustrated. As submitted, the results cannot be independently verified.

The custom 'Energy Efficiency' metric (Eq. 2) is ad hoc: latency is passed through an arbitrary sigmoid activation with an unspecified sensitivity coefficient γ, and utilization penalties use an unmotivated exponential form. No justification or sensitivity analysis for γ is given, and all headline energy-efficiency claims (Figure 11) depend on this non-standard metric, which weakens comparability with prior work.

The optimization evaluation is narrow: HLSTuner is tested on only five PolyBench kernels, all small linear-algebra routines with reported resource utilization under ~4% (Table 2), i.e., far from resource-constrained regimes despite the 'resource-constrained kernels' framing in the abstract. Five kernels plus a proxy metric is thin evidence for the claim of 'strong generalization potential'.

Baseline comparisons are potentially uneven: DSL baselines (Dahlia, HeteroCL, Allo) require rewriting designs in a different language, while HLSTuner operates on existing HLS-C; the claimed speedups may partially reflect differences in the underlying generated hardware rather than optimization quality. The '3.6× average over SOTA' claim in the abstract aggregates heterogeneous baselines without clarifying per-baseline conditions (attempt budgets, host code, interface overhead).

Several methodological details are under-specified: how the 612 test cases and '15 manually crafted designs' were constructed and who verified gold labels; how 'All experiments were excluded from the training distribution' is guaranteed for the Manual set; and how the scoring agent (LLM 6) selects among candidate fixes, which directly affects the reported pass rates.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Figure 3 is overloaded with ten LLM agents and duplicated graphical elements; Figure 2 lacks a described evaluation protocol for the surveyed LLMs; and the paper contains typographical errors ('optimzation', 'Abaltion Study') suggesting insufficient polish.

Novelty relative to very recent work is incremental: fine-tuned LLM repair loops for HLS exist (e.g., Xu et al. 2024b, Gai et al. 2025), and the main deltas—bug-injection data augmentation and a multi-agent fallback path—are plausible but not rigorously isolated against the strongest recent baselines at equal compute.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated, clearly articulated problem: LLMs struggle with HLS-specific synthesizability constraints, directive semantics, and QoR-aware directive tuning, and the paper decomposes this into three concrete challenges.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this genre of systems paper: staged pass@k metrics across CSIM/CSYN/COSIM, per-error-type breakdowns (Figure 14, Table 5), ablations isolating fixing vs. analysis vs. DPO vs. multi-LLM judging, matched RAG baselines (Table 8/9), a train-test similarity (Rouge-L) analysis to rule out data leakage, post-Place-and-Route validity checks (Table 4), and token-cost comparisons.

The core ideas are sensible and well-executed: reasoning-to-instruction debugging with tool-grounded error feedback, QoR-aware CoT supervision distilled from verified (rather than LLM-invented) results, and a self-evolving error repository (BugRAG/VODA) for dataset construction.

Restricting HLSTuner to directive-level transformations while preserving kernel semantics is a defensible and clearly justified design decision, avoiding the correctness hazards of LLM code rewriting.

The limitation section is candid (no DATAFLOW/interface support, single FPGA target), and the appendix provides enough training detail (model, optimizer, epochs, LR schedules, hardware) to support reproduction in principle.
weaknesses: Relevance to the ACL audience is marginal: the paper is fundamentally an EDA/FPGA design-automation contribution (HLS, directives, RTL synthesis, DSP/LUT utilization) that uses LLMs as components. The NLP content (SFT, DPO, CoT distillation, RAG) is standard and not the scientific contribution; the work seems better suited to an LLM-aided-design or CAD venue (several baselines come from ICLAD/ICCAD/DAC).

Reproducibility is uncertain: no explicit statement that the fine-tuned models, BugRAG repository, injected-error test sets, or pipeline code will be released. Much of the framework depends on proprietary/closed LLMs (Gemini-3-pro, DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-5, Claude) accessed via API, whose versions and behaviors are non-stationary.

The debugging benchmark is self-constructed by the same authors using the same error-injection taxonomy (Table 5's 34 error types) used for training. Although the authors argue the injected samples are unique and unseen, the evaluation risks rewarding the model on exactly the synthetic error distribution it was trained on; results may not transfer to organic HLS errors.

The headline 3.3× speedup over RALAD relies on the authors' own reproduction of RALAD (with a different backbone, GPT-5.1), and baseline details such as prompts, budgets, and tuning effort for competitor methods are only partially specified; comparisons against C2HLSC/HLSRewriter reuse published numbers obtained under different settings.

The 10-agent/LLM-group architecture (LLMs 1–10) feels over-engineered, and the paper does not disentangle the contribution of the multi-agent orchestration itself versus the fine-tuned specialists; several components (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge refinement) contribute only a few percent and their necessity is unclear.

Some reported gains are presented inconsistently (e.g., 32.6% appears as both 'debugging improvement' in the abstract and 'error analysis accuracy' in the contributions; 41.8% vs. 37% in different places), and several figures are dense and hard to read, slightly weakening clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: LLMs struggle with HLS-specific synthesizability constraints and directive semantics, and the presented error taxonomy (Tables 1 and 5, 33+ error types) is a useful artifact in its own right.

Evaluation is grounded in a real vendor toolchain (Vitis HLS 2022.1) with the full CSIM/CSYN/COSIM verification stack, and Table 4 additionally validates designs after Place-and-Route, which rules out purely synthetic latency gains from infeasible unrolling.

The appendix includes a controlled RAG-baseline study (Tables 8 and 9) that partially addresses fairness concerns about comparing a specialized pipeline against general-purpose LLMs, and reports the somewhat surprising finding that documentation RAG can hurt early-stage correctness.

Reasonable ablation coverage (Figures 7 and 16): the individual contributions of the analysis agent, DPO, and multi-LLM judging are separated, and a model-scale study (Qwen2.5-Coder vs. Qwen3 across 1.5B–14B) adds evidence that gains come from fine-tuning rather than scale alone.
Resource-budgeted optimization objective (utilization ≤ 80%) and a 1-hour synthesis timeout make the HLSTuner comparison somewhat more principled than unconstrained speedup reporting.
weaknesses: The headline debugging result (93.4% pass@1) is essentially an in-distribution evaluation. The 591 test cases are constructed by injecting the same error taxonomy (34 error types from Table 5) used to build the 10,878 training samples, via the same automated injection technique, and from the same Kernel/Vitis design pools. A fine-tuned model trained on synthetic instances of these exact error patterns is expected to score highly; the result does not establish generalization to real HLS errors that practitioners encounter. The Rouge-L similarity analysis (Appendix D.1) measures surface similarity of code, not independence of the error-generation process.

Relevance to the ACL/NLP community is marginal. The core contributions are in hardware design automation (HLS directive tuning, toolchain-verified debugging); the NLP techniques employed (SFT, DPO, multi-agent orchestration, RAG, LLM-as-judge) are standard and not adapted or analyzed in a way that yields transferable insight for computational linguistics.

Novelty is incremental: each component (multi-agent debugging, tool-feedback-grounded repair, NSGA-II-generated QoR data, teacher-generated CoT, DPO, VODA-style error accumulation) is a known technique, and the paper does not clearly isolate what is conceptually new beyond careful engineering. Notably, VODA — one of the four claimed contributions — has no dedicated ablation quantifying its benefit.

HLSTuner's optimization training uses 20 Rosetta kernels while the speedup evaluation (Figure 9) uses largely the same family of PolyBench-style kernels (atax, bicg, gemm, mvt, ...). Even if code-level similarity is low, tuning policies for well-known kernels with well-known optimal pragmas raise a memorization concern the paper itself gestures at when diagnosing DeepSeek-V3.2 as 'trivially memorized' — but does not exclude for its own model.

Baseline asymmetry persists despite the RAG controls: ChatHLS uses multiple fine-tuned agents plus tool feedback plus retries, while general LLM baselines are single-shot or lightly scaffolded. The '3.3× speedup over RALAD' claim also depends on reproduced baselines (RALAD re-run with GPT-5.1) whose fidelity to the original systems is unverifiable.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or dataset release is stated, training data are distilled from a closed commercial model (DeepSeek-V3.2), and several crucial details (exact prompts for candidate generation in the LLM-as-judge loop, bug-injection validation rate, per-kernel trial statistics) are only partially specified.

Some quantitative claims are imprecise or internally inconsistent: '41.8% improvement in generation success rate' is a relative comparison against Gemini-3-pro at one stage of a multi-stage pipeline; the debugging headline (32.6%) and generation headline (41.8%) refer to different comparisons, which inflates the perceived scope of improvement. The paper also cites several 2026-dated references, which weakens verifiability.

The limitation section acknowledges that DATAFLOW and AXI interface directives — central to deployable FPGA designs — are unsupported, which narrows the practical impact of the 'agile hardware development' framing considerably.

strengths: Comprehensive and unusually careful experimental design for a systems paper: staged verification metrics (CSIM/CSYN/COSIM), pass@k with unbiased estimation, controlled RAG baselines that isolate retrieval from model adaptation (Appendix E), ablations decomposing the debugging pipeline (fixing vs. analysis vs. DPO vs. multi-agent judging), and train-test similarity analysis (Rouge-L) to argue against data leakage.

The VODA/BugRAG verification-oriented data augmentation idea is a sensible and somewhat novel approach to the documented scarcity of HLS-specific error data, and the self-evolving error-case expansion is a reusable contribution.

Evaluation goes beyond synthesis-level numbers: post-implementation (place-and-route) validation confirms the reported latency gains are physically realizable, and resource-utilization budgets are enforced in the speedup metric rather than ignored.
The paper is transparent about limitations (no DATAFLOW/AXI support, single FPGA target, single HLS tool version), which increases confidence in the reported claims within their stated scope.
Token-consumption analysis and runtime budgets give practical context that the improvements come at acceptable cost.

Strong empirical gains are consistent across multiple independent benchmarks (HLS-Eval, PolyBench-derived kernels, accelerators like MobileNet/Transformer) rather than a single cherry-picked workload.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the debugging evaluation: HLSFixer training data and the 591 debugging test cases are both produced by the same automated bug-injection procedure over the same error taxonomy (33-34 types from the same BugRAG repository). Although Rouge-L similarity is reported, the shared injection methodology and error-type distribution structurally advantage the fine-tuned analysis agent; the gains over RAG-augmented general LLMs may therefore be partially inflated. Test bugs injected by a different process or harvested from real user forums would substantially strengthen the claim.

Reproducibility is limited: no artifact/code/dataset release is indicated anywhere in the manuscript, the pipeline depends on proprietary API models (DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini-3-pro, GPT-5.1, Claude-opus-4.5) and a commercial tool (Vitis HLS 2022.1), and the full system spans ~10 specialized LLM agents whose orchestration details are hard to reconstruct. For a Findings-level contribution the detailed hyperparameters and prompts help, but independent replication would be very difficult as submitted.

Venue fit is a genuine concern: the paper is an LLM-for-EDA/systems contribution (HLS pragma tuning and synthesis-log debugging). While it uses standard NLP techniques (SFT, DPO, CoT distillation, RAG), there is little linguistic or NLP-methodological insight that would transfer; it would fit ICLAD/ICCAD/DAC more naturally.

Novelty relative to prior LLM-for-HLS work (RALAD, HLSPilot, HLSDebugger, C2HLSC, HLSRewriter, LIFT) is primarily integrative: the individual components (fine-tuned repair agent, judge ensemble, QoR-aware CoT, RAG over docs) are each established techniques. The main technical novelty rests on VODA and the reasoning-to-instruction decomposition, which are not deeply analyzed (e.g., no analysis of when the judge system helps vs. hurts, and the DPO construction rationale in Sec. 3.3 is confusingly written).

Some reporting inconsistencies and presentation issues: contribution bullets and abstract cite different headline numbers (32.6%, 41.8%, 3.3x) without a single consolidated summary table; Figure 3 is overloaded and difficult to parse; the ablation percentages in Sec. 4.3.2 (16.6%, 3.7%, 16.5%) are not clearly defined relative to the Figure 7 bars.

Comparisons with external baselines (C2HLSC, HLSRewriter) reuse their reported numbers under possibly different tool versions and settings rather than re-running them, which weakens direct comparability, and the RALAD reproduction relies on a different backbone (GPT-5.1).

The claimed 'QoR-aware reasoning' is trained on teacher-generated explanations of already-verified solutions, so it is unclear whether the CoT actually mediates decisions or is post-hoc; no experiment (e.g., reasoning ablation or probing) directly validates that the causal reasoning, rather than imitation of directive patterns, drives the optimization gains.
